A receptacle is any object — a container, a slot, a holder, or a space — that is designed or used to receive and hold something else.

Think of it this way: a receptacle is a passive object. Its whole job is to sit there and accept whatever is placed into it or attached to it. It doesn't act — it simply receives.

In its most common, everyday use, a receptacle is just a container meant for holding things, especially for collecting or storing them:

  • A trash can is a receptacle for garbage.
  • A basket at a donation drive is a receptacle for clothes or food.
  • A bowl placed on a table to collect keys and coins is a receptacle.
  • A box for collecting ballot papers at a polling station is a receptacle.

When people use the word receptacle instead of simply saying "container" or "bin," they often mean something slightly more formal, deliberate, or official. You'd see it on signage — "Please deposit used materials in the receptacle provided" — rather than in casual conversation with a friend.
What Makes It Different From Just "Container"?

The word carries two key ideas that a plain word like "container" or "box" doesn't always carry:

  1. Designed to receive. A receptacle is made for the purpose of holding something. It implies intention. A random bag lying on the floor isn't typically called a receptacle; a designated collection bin is.
  2. Passivity. A receptacle just sits and accepts. It doesn't transform, process, or send. It simply holds. This sense of passive acceptance is baked into the word.

So while every receptacle is a container, not every container feels quite right to call a receptacle. You'd call a hospital waste bin a receptacle — it's formal, it's designated, it passively collects. You'd probably just call a lunch box a "box."

In the context of electricity and electrical wiring — especially in North American English — a receptacle refers to the power outlet in your wall: the slot where you plug in a phone charger, a lamp, or any electrical device.

  • "The electrician installed a new receptacle near the kitchen counter."
  • "This receptacle is a three-prong outlet rated for 15 amperes."

In everyday speech, people usually just say "outlet" or "socket." But in technical, professional, and official contexts — building codes, electrical manuals, product descriptions — the correct term is receptacle. The logic is the same: the outlet receives the plug of an electrical device.

In botany (the science of plants), a receptacle has a very specific meaning: it is the thickened, fleshy end of the flower stalk — the part of the stem that the flower sits on and to which all the flower's parts (petals, stamens, sepals, pistil) are attached.

Think of it as the platform that holds the flower together at its base. In some plants, the receptacle becomes part of what we eat. In a strawberry, for example, the red fleshy part you eat is actually the enlarged, swollen receptacle — the true fruits are the tiny seed-like dots on the surface. In a fig, the entire fruit is essentially a hollow, fleshy receptacle that contains hundreds of tiny flowers inside it.
Register and Tone: When and Where People Use This Word

Receptacle sits on the formal to technical end of the language spectrum. You'll encounter it more in:

  • Written signs and notices ("Please use the receptacle provided")
  • Legal or regulatory documents
  • Scientific and technical writing (botany, electrical engineering, chemistry)
  • Formal descriptions of equipment or infrastructure

You're unlikely to hear it in casual, everyday conversation. Nobody says to a friend, "Toss it in the receptacle." They say, "Throw it in the bin."

This doesn't mean receptacle is a rare or obscure word — it's perfectly common and widely understood. It simply belongs to a slightly elevated register.
A Subtlety Worth Noting: Receptacle vs. Vessel vs. Repository

These words are all in the same family of meaning, but with different shades:

  • A vessel often implies something that carries or transports (a ship, a blood vessel, a jar for liquid).
  • A repository implies a place where things are stored and can be retrieved later — it emphasizes storage and access (a repository of knowledge, a data repository).
  • A receptacle emphasizes the act of receiving and holding — it's the most neutral of the three, and is often used for physical objects that collect things placed into them.

These show the word used naturally across different contexts:

  • "The city installed new recycling receptacles on every street corner."
  • "Make sure the electrical receptacle is grounded before plugging in the equipment."
  • "The botanist explained that the receptacle of a rose is the green bulge just below the petals."
  • "During the ceremony, guests dropped their written wishes into a decorative receptacle at the entrance."
  • "The lab technician disposed of the used syringes in a sharps receptacle."

A receptacle is anything that passively receives and holds something else — be it a trash bin, a wall outlet, or the base of a flower. The word is formal in tone and correct in contexts that call for precision: official signage, technical writing, science, and electrical work. Across all its uses, the core idea remains unchanged: it is an object whose purpose is simply to receive.
